LAND REALITY

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The issue of expropriation without compensation has inflamed emotions causing a worldwide debate. But we are going to look at the first farm that is CONFIRMED to be up for expropriation and the realit

Unique Selling Point:
Johan Steenkamp’s farm is being expropriated. He’s a well-known avocado farmer and founder of Peppadew in South Africa. He is a co-owner of Akkerland Boerdery, which farms on two properties, Lukin and Salaita, near Njeledam behind Soutpansberg. His business partner is his brother-in-law, Arnold Cloete. He says they are happy to sell the land for fair market value, but they are currently involved in two court battles – one against the expropriation of land involving the Musekwa community, and another to fight the expropriation without compensation of our land. Akkerland Boerdery was originally offered an allegedly ridiculous amount of money as compensation, after the land was initially expropriated in favour of the Musekwa community. According to Steenkamp, the offer was neither reasonable nor accurate in terms of the market value of the property, and they started a process to ascertain the legality of the offer in court. Even before this expropriation process began, the new minister of rural development and land reform, Maite Nkoana-Mashabane, let Akkerland know their farms would be expropriated. The court documents were delivered a day before Easter weekend, and they were given just seven days to hand over the keys to their farms. After an emergency interdict against the minister, a process is now under way to set aside the entire expropriation process involving the two farms. The Musekwa community do not have a title deed to the Lukin and Salaita farms. The Kuvule community, by contrast, produced allegedly legitimate title deeds to the land long before the expropriation took place. Their lawyers, Denga Incorporated, have confirmed the view that it is in fact their clients who have actual rights to the land. But there are also allegations that the mining corporation Coal of Africa may in fact be behind the expropriation action, and that this has nothing to do with historical land reform, and everything to do with mining. It is common knowledge that the Lukin and Salaita farms form part of the valuable coal belt in the region. This is the where the land expropriate fight is currently taking place – it’s not theoretical. Please also see below that Steenkamps neighbour’s property was part of a land claim and it’s now in ruins – that community will also speak.

Summary:
According to Ernst Roets of AfriForum, minister of land development and reform Maite Nkoana-Mashabane said they put together a list of 139 farms earmarked for land expropriation without compensation. This has become a hotly contested debate. In Limpopo nine farms are earmarked for expropriation - Akkerland Broerdery’s farm is on the Afriforum list, but AgriSA are questioning the legitimacy of the list, adding that making the list public was irresponsible. According to AgriSA, a snap survey of the list exposed its inaccuracy, which could have been legitimized before it was made public. Investigations conducted by AfriSA’s affiliations show that some farms on the list are those belonging to black farmers with joint procurement. We would also speak to AFASA in Midrand - who are the African Farmers Association of South Africa – who will say how this will also affect black farmers as well – not just white farmers, and there are black farmers on the list.



Further information:
A detailed study shows how much land government owns, which could be used in land restitution – which is what Cyril Ramaphosa said earlier this year in SONA 2018. A preliminary constitutional review committee report shows 59% of submissions are not in favour of land expropriation, and Ralph Mathekga can talk about it (we already have the footage) - analysis on ANC and Parly headed for confrontation about above report. The ANC's own constituents don't list land ownership as their top 5 concerns. Zuma’s SONA 2017 address says 90% of people would prefer cash to land. The major concern is that government have failed in so many of its undertakings – especially its past land claim cases (for example the tea plantation next to Akkerland Broedery won the plantation in a land claim and it’s lying in ruin, that community will speak because no one assisted them in running it etc) Besides the obvious food security issues… The need for land restitution and a look at the success of the process – we would speak to experts: farmers weekly – who have a fair view on this issue – Chris Burgess – very progressive. And also Ralph Mathekga as well, and we would have the study.
Land facts from the land audit report: comm. 5302
LINK: 17,439 million ha has been transferred from white ownership since 1994 – 21% of the 82,758 million ha of farmland in freehold SA.
27 feb 2018 National Assembly made landmark decision to review section 25 of the constitution in order to cater for the principle of land expropriation without compensation.
This followed the decision by the ANC in December 2017 and the elective conference where it indicated it would start the process towards a constitutional amendment to make land redistribution possible without compensation – provided that it was sustainable and doesn’t harm the agricultural section or economy.
What does the DATA say?
Distributed: 4 850 100 ha
Restored via restitution claims: 3 389 727 ha
The equivalent area for which financial compensation was chosen is 2 772 457 ha
Thus a total of 11 million ha have been redistributed through gov programs. The state owns more than 4,000 farms which makes up of 4,027 million ha according to 2015 State Land Audit. The total land moved out of white ownership = 15,039 million ha.
LINK: This is because 90% of claimants opted for money rather than land – according to President Zuma in Sona 2017.
Provincial land audits show, (research uni of Pretoria), that the department of rural development and land reform – ask Ralph Mathekga to explain… Roughly 17,439 MILLION HA has been transferred from white ownership since 1994.

LINK: Only 4% of farms in south Africa generate a turnover of R5 million – most farms are in debt mostly 30-50% of their lands value. Who will inherit the debt?

LINK: 80,000 land restitution claims have been lodged – 70% urban, 30% rural. It’s actually an urban issue.
94% of our country is registered at the deeds office – only 6% of our land is available…
Land audit reveals whites own 72% of total farms and agricultural holdings – and africans own 4%.
According to Chris: Not sure I understand about the interview. What info would you like me to send? I think the basic point is that the state has done close to bugger all about land reform for the last 23 years, and now wants to pin the problem on farmers. (We spent more money on protecting politicians last year, than buying farms for black farmers. That should about sum it up). The high-level report of former president Kgalema Monthlante also makes it crystal clear that the problem with land reform is corruption and mismanagement of the state, but that somehow never gets mentioned. We hosted the land summit out of sheer frustration and to showcase what commercial agriculture has achieved as far as transformational efforts are concerned, despite the state. The unintended result of the conference was an outpouring of goodwill from both black and white farmers, and a genuine willingness to make things work. The sort of constructive attitude that the state seems to purposefully and rather cynically sabotage for short term political gain. Bottom line is, if you want land reform to work, let the farmers do it (as Nick Serfontein, the big Free State farmer explained to Cyril in his open letter that went viral, and who today sits on the president’s advisory panel), because farmers know what it takes to farm. Bureaucrats in Pretoria don’t. Black farmers also need title to their land to be able to raise capital to fund their operations, which doesn’t happen. This is all not rocket science, but I think we truly underestimate how thoroughly useless the state is, and the terrible danger that doing nothing holds for the entire country.

Press Release:


Expropriation Without Compensation
After 20 years and R40-billion spent, the government says land reform has taken too long and experts say some redistributed farms have failed. Now, amid a polarising tug of war fuelled by misinformation, rhetoric and fear, government is trying to forge a way forward to address historical injustices through land expropriation without compensation. But what does it mean when land claimants obtain the land, without the business and resources to make it profitable?
Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein
Presenter: Claire Mawisa
Researcher: Sinethemba Nogude


Script:


The land expropriation without compensation debate has polarized South Africans (Examples)
And has now spread to the international twitter feed of Donald Trump and Australia’s Land Affairs Minister.
Newsreaders: “Trump...Australia upsounds.”
CLAIRE LINK: “STOP! THE EMOTIVE TOPIC OF LAND IN SOUTH AFRICA IS NOT JUST A BLACK AND WHITE ISSUE, THE CONVERSATION AROUND EXPROPRIATION WITHOUT COMPENSATION HAS BEEN FILLED WITH MISINFORMATION, PROVOCATIVE STATEMENTS AND RHETORIC. HOW WILL IT WORK, WHOSE ENTITLED TO THE LAND, SHOULD FARMERS BE AFRAID, WHAT’S THE REAL STORY?”
It was at the December 2017 ANC elective conference that the party resolved to expropriate land without compensation. A public participation process soon followed.
UPSOUND: Cyril Ramaphosa: “The expropriation without compensation land is envisages as one of the measures that we will use to accelerate the redistribution of land to black South Africans.”
At the National Council of Provinces debate this week, President Cyril Ramaphosa reiterated government’s stance to investigate whether the constitution’s expropriation bill should incorporate land expropriation without compensation.
But some may be surprised that the move to test the constitutionality of expropriation was already made in March this year.
THAT’s when experienced avocado farmer, Johan Steenkamp, received a letter from government giving him just 7 days to hand over the keys to Akkerland Boerdery - a hunting concession in Soutpansberg, Limpopo – he also co-owns.
As Akkerland sits on a R70 billion coal deposit, he says he refused governments offer of R20 million because the property’s market value is R200 million.
Steenkamp: “I will come to your house, I’ll give you R1,000 for your house, but if you don’t it to me for R1,000, I’m taking it, and that’s, that’s so sad.”
Government says they cannot comment as the Akkerland case is currently in court and therefore subjudice.
Steenkamp: “It’s politically driven. I bought all my properties like every other farmer legally. The narrative by political parties that it’s been stolen is completely false.”
National House of Traditional Leaders Chairperson Ikosi Sipho Mahlangu says land was taken through conquest, from blacks and given to whites as a reward.
Mahlangu: “If land was given to you for free, you’ve developed the land, you’ve extracted value out of the land, what stops you from handing it back? If ppl have done improvements on the land then you can be paid for the improvement done, but you can’t be paid for the land.”
In parliament, Mahlangu - who is also a traditional leader - made submissions as to why land should be expropriated without compensation.
Mahlangu: “We had to take parliament down memory lane, in terms of where, the issues of dispossession started with the wars that had been fought, they were killed for that land, and they were made slaves on their own land.”
Political analyst Ralph Mathekga explains why the history of land is contentious.
Mathekga: “I think that at the centre of this is a political issue, as to how do we settle our historical squabbles in relation to land, the whole idea of dispossession and identity of a majority of black people, their identity has been denied by taking away of that land.”
In August the partial results of parliament’s public participation process showed that 59% of the submissions were against changing the constitution.
Mathekga: “If you are solving this problem by just returning land you are failing to understand the demand of a modern citizen; is a modern citizen interested in farming?”
CLAIRE LINK: 80,000 LAND RESTITUTION CLAIMS HAVE BEEN LODGED, 70% URBAN AND 30% RURAL - IT’S ACTUALLY AN URBAN ISSUE.
Ralph: “It’s not framed in a way that deals with the comprehensive problems; the economy, lack of rural economic development, the problem of urban housing, the problem of lack of spatial development planning in this country. Each and every young person who is in rural areas, their destiny is urban areas because, there is no productivity in that area. Expropriating land is not going to solve those problems.”
But if you want to understand land reform, the best place to look is on the ground with the farmers who are on the frontlines of expropriation.
Black Farmer: “I’m not a farmer as my mentor mentioned to me yesterday, I am now a producer!”
Welcome to the August Landbouweekblad land summit… Unions and farmers of all races had conversations about expropriation.
White farmer: “It was a hard-nosed farmers who never believed that those guys in the black communal areas could come up to a commercial level, in terms of those hectares that they got, and guys we’ve done it!”
Landbouweekblad editor Chris Burgess says the conversations moved outside of the polarized political landscape.
Claire: “Why decide to convene a land summit?”
Chris: “It’s out of sheer frustration really, about the superficiality of the land debate. We spent more on protecting politicians – than buying land for black farmers.”
CLAIRE LINK: GETTING LAND, IS NOT THE SAME AS GETTING A FARM, THE ACTUAL VALUE OF THE LAND IS ONLY 10% OF THE ACTUAL VALUE OF THE FARM, WITHOUT THE PROPER INFRASTRUCTURE, EXPERTISE. JUST GETTING LANDING FOR AN EMERGING FARMER MEANS NOTHING.
Prince Makgoba: “When our late great grandfather used to occupy this land, he was assassinated and his head was chopped.”
Prince Mike Makgoba is part of the Makgoba tribe’s royal family.
Mike Makgoba: “Our land was taken, our community was then scattered all over the country.
The tribe was awarded land including this historic tea estate near Magoebaskloof, Limpopo. The Makgoba’s, like many other claimants, didn’t’ realize they were only awarded the land.
Prince Makgoba: “The farm was already dead, all the movables, tractors, irrigation, equipment, the pumps were all auctioned.”
African Farmers Association of South Africa President Dr. Vuyo Mahlati says their members have complained that they are not given title deeds, and therefore cannot acquire financing.
Dr. Vuyo Mahlathi: “There were very serious issues in terms of title deeds not having them, and infrastructure, the water rights generally resides with the white commercial farmers.”
CLAIRE LINK: “GETTING THE LAND BACK IS NOT JUST ABOUT THE SOIL, LAND OWNERSHIP IS A TANGIBLE AND MEANINGFUL WAY TO GET INVOLVED IN THE ECONOMY.”
Dr. Mahlati: “On one hand you’re dealing with property rights and they want to hold onto them and protect and defend at all costs, and on the other hand, you have those who have no access to those rights and are looking - and these are the majority of the people.”
Ralph: “We don’t recognize that it is a historical issue, we tend to juxtapose it with our intention to deal with our economic problem, making sure that we ensure economic participation of the previously disadvantaged.”
Rural Development and Land Reform’s Acting Director General Rendani Sadiki says government have stayed in line with the current constitution.
Sadiki: “We’ve been expropriating and giving the land back to owner and settling with farmer. Until such time when there is a law that says you can expropriate without compensation.”
overnments 2017 land audit report which looked only ar title deeds shows the majority of land is privately owned – predominantly made up of companies and trusts, and therefore the owners could not be established. However, less than a third of the land is owned by individuals, and the government broke down these numbers.
Sadiki: “The land audit indicated that 72% was owned by white, and about 4% black owned. Now our minister has ordered that we do a phase three that will unbundle it further.”
But Organized Agriculture, the land bank and many other organizations question the government's numbers. President of the World Farmers Organisation Dr. Theo de Jager explains why.
De Jager: “The vast majority of farmers in South Africa do not trust that audit. It is not as easy as going to the deeds office and looking at the names there.”
Chris: “Do we need to go further than the high panel investigation of former-president Kgalema Motlanthe? The problems with land reform are corruption, bureaucratic bungling - that report is there.”
CLAIRE LINK: SINCE 1994, ONLY 21% OF FARMLAND IN FREEHOLD SOUTH AFRICA HAS BEEN TRANSFERRED FROM WHITE OWNERSHIP, BUT SOME ARGUE THAT SINCE LAND CLAIMANTS PREFERRED CASH OVER LAND, THAT PERCENTAGE COULD BE MUCH HIGHER.
According to government 90% of land claims are currently settled through financial compensation.
Dr. Vuyo: “The current status quo is not feasible, and if you start from that premise, and understanding THAT - there is no freedom without justice on land.”
Farmers want the “just and equitable” compensation clause of the expropriation bill in the constitution to be more clearly defined as they would like market value for their properties.
de Jager: “We are not scared about the expropriation, it’s about the compensation part of it. Because then we would know that there’s fair value being paid, nobody would be paid too much. Or too less in the process, and also it enables the land own owner who loses the land to re-establish himself elsewhere.”
Steenkamp: “It’s the same as going to somebody and saying I’m taking away your future. 11:32:28 But not only taking away your future, but taking away all my farmer workers futures 11:32:34 and their children, you’re taking away families future, not only me. And as a whole in south Africa we’ve all seen where the rand as gone in the past few weeks, destructive and this thing will spiral dive until it’s resolved. 11:32:49
Sadiki: “We have spent 40 billion so far on restitution alone, which is very expensive, and I think at some point we need to agree that this exercise is going to take forever, and the constitution says government you have a responsibility to makes sure all your there’s access to land by all your citizens.”
Mahlangu: “Government has tried to come up with many laws to be able to transform the land reform, but most of them have not been properly implemented, but also there’s been constitutional stumbling blocks.”
Carte Blanche found that everyone was exceptionally guarded about the issue of expropriation without compensation, which only shows how difficult it is to separate emotions from this complex issue.
Claire: “How would you like to see the expropriation of land without compensation roll out?”
de Jager: “We should not expropriate any land without compensation. There’s just in no kind of democracy you can imagine, demanding from an individual to pick up the bill for a national imperative.”
Mahlangu: “Land must be expropriated, but when it’s expropriate it let there be a thought process on how we’re going to do it”
Chris: “Sometimes we wonder if the land question isn’t purposefully being held back so that the politicians have got a stick to beat ppl with.”
Dr. Mahlati: “Land is emotional, we’re talking about social justice, identity and belonging. And if you don’t have land you don’t belong.”

Title Author Last Updated 16 September 2018 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 21 September 2018 Press Release: Expropriation Without Compensation After 20 years and R40-billion spent, the government says land reform has taken too long and experts say some redistributed farms have failed. Now, amid a polarising tug of war fuelled by misinformation, rhetoric and fear, government is trying to forge a way forward to address historical injustices through land expropriation without compensation. But what does it mean when land claimants obtain the land, without the business and resources to make it profitable? Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein Presenter: Claire Mawisa Researcher: Sinethemba Nogude Script: The land expropriation without compensation debate has polarized South Africans (Examples) And has now spread to the international twitter feed of Donald Trump and Australia’s Land Affairs Minister. Newsreaders: “Trump...Australia upsounds.” CLAIRE LINK: “STOP! THE EMOTIVE TOPIC OF LAND IN SOUTH AFRICA IS NOT JUST A BLACK AND WHITE ISSUE, THE CONVERSATION AROUND EXPROPRIATION WITHOUT COMPENSATION HAS BEEN FILLED WITH MISINFORMATION, PROVOCATIVE STATEMENTS AND RHETORIC. HOW WILL IT WORK, WHOSE ENTITLED TO THE LAND, SHOULD FARMERS BE AFRAID, WHAT’S THE REAL STORY?” It was at the December 2017 ANC elective conference that the party resolved to expropriate land without compensation. A public participation process soon followed. UPSOUND: Cyril Ramaphosa: “The expropriation without compensation land is envisages as one of the measures that we will use to accelerate the redistribution of land to black South Africans.” At the National Council of Provinces debate this week, President Cyril Ramaphosa reiterated government’s stance to investigate whether the constitution’s expropriation bill should incorporate land expropriation without compensation. But some may be surprised that the move to test the constitutionality of expropriation was already made in March this year. THAT’s when experienced avocado farmer, Johan Steenkamp, received a letter from government giving him just 7 days to hand over the keys to Akkerland Boerdery - a hunting concession in Soutpansberg, Limpopo – he also co-owns. As Akkerland sits on a R70 billion coal deposit, he says he refused governments offer of R20 million because the property’s market value is R200 million. Steenkamp: “I will come to your house, I’ll give you R1,000 for your house, but if you don’t it to me for R1,000, I’m taking it, and that’s, that’s so sad.” Government says they cannot comment as the Akkerland case is currently in court and therefore subjudice. Steenkamp: “It’s politically driven. I bought all my properties like every other farmer legally. The narrative by political parties that it’s been stolen is completely false.” National House of Traditional Leaders Chairperson Ikosi Sipho Mahlangu says land was taken through conquest, from blacks and given to whites as a reward. Mahlangu: “If land was given to you for free, you’ve developed the land, you’ve extracted value out of the land, what stops you from handing it back? If ppl have done improvements on the land then you can be paid for the improvement done, but you can’t be paid for the land.” In parliament, Mahlangu - who is also a traditional leader - made submissions as to why land should be expropriated without compensation. Mahlangu: “We had to take parliament down memory lane, in terms of where, the issues of dispossession started with the wars that had been fought, they were killed for that land, and they were made slaves on their own land.” Political analyst Ralph Mathekga explains why the history of land is contentious. Mathekga: “I think that at the centre of this is a political issue, as to how do we settle our historical squabbles in relation to land, the whole idea of dispossession and identity of a majority of black people, their identity has been denied by taking away of that land.” In August the partial results of parliament’s public participation process showed that 59% of the submissions were against changing the constitution. Mathekga: “If you are solving this problem by just returning land you are failing to understand the demand of a modern citizen; is a modern citizen interested in farming?” CLAIRE LINK: 80,000 LAND RESTITUTION CLAIMS HAVE BEEN LODGED, 70% URBAN AND 30% RURAL - IT’S ACTUALLY AN URBAN ISSUE. Ralph: “It’s not framed in a way that deals with the comprehensive problems; the economy, lack of rural economic development, the problem of urban housing, the problem of lack of spatial development planning in this country. Each and every young person who is in rural areas, their destiny is urban areas because, there is no productivity in that area. Expropriating land is not going to solve those problems.” But if you want to understand land reform, the best place to look is on the ground with the farmers who are on the frontlines of expropriation. Black Farmer: “I’m not a farmer as my mentor mentioned to me yesterday, I am now a producer!” Welcome to the August Landbouweekblad land summit… Unions and farmers of all races had conversations about expropriation. White farmer: “It was a hard-nosed farmers who never believed that those guys in the black communal areas could come up to a commercial level, in terms of those hectares that they got, and guys we’ve done it!” Landbouweekblad editor Chris Burgess says the conversations moved outside of the polarized political landscape. Claire: “Why decide to convene a land summit?” Chris: “It’s out of sheer frustration really, about the superficiality of the land debate. We spent more on protecting politicians – than buying land for black farmers.” CLAIRE LINK: GETTING LAND, IS NOT THE SAME AS GETTING A FARM, THE ACTUAL VALUE OF THE LAND IS ONLY 10% OF THE ACTUAL VALUE OF THE FARM, WITHOUT THE PROPER INFRASTRUCTURE, EXPERTISE. JUST GETTING LANDING FOR AN EMERGING FARMER MEANS NOTHING. Prince Makgoba: “When our late great grandfather used to occupy this land, he was assassinated and his head was chopped.” Prince Mike Makgoba is part of the Makgoba tribe’s royal family. Mike Makgoba: “Our land was taken, our community was then scattered all over the country. The tribe was awarded land including this historic tea estate near Magoebaskloof, Limpopo. The Makgoba’s, like many other claimants, didn’t’ realize they were only awarded the land. Prince Makgoba: “The farm was already dead, all the movables, tractors, irrigation, equipment, the pumps were all auctioned.” African Farmers Association of South Africa President Dr. Vuyo Mahlati says their members have complained that they are not given title deeds, and therefore cannot acquire financing. Dr. Vuyo Mahlathi: “There were very serious issues in terms of title deeds not having them, and infrastructure, the water rights generally resides with the white commercial farmers.” CLAIRE LINK: “GETTING THE LAND BACK IS NOT JUST ABOUT THE SOIL, LAND OWNERSHIP IS A TANGIBLE AND MEANINGFUL WAY TO GET INVOLVED IN THE ECONOMY.” Dr. Mahlati: “On one hand you’re dealing with property rights and they want to hold onto them and protect and defend at all costs, and on the other hand, you have those who have no access to those rights and are looking - and these are the majority of the people.” Ralph: “We don’t recognize that it is a historical issue, we tend to juxtapose it with our intention to deal with our economic problem, making sure that we ensure economic participation of the previously disadvantaged.” Rural Development and Land Reform’s Acting Director General Rendani Sadiki says government have stayed in line with the current constitution. Sadiki: “We’ve been expropriating and giving the land back to owner and settling with farmer. Until such time when there is a law that says you can expropriate without compensation.” overnments 2017 land audit report which looked only ar title deeds shows the majority of land is privately owned – predominantly made up of companies and trusts, and therefore the owners could not be established. However, less than a third of the land is owned by individuals, and the government broke down these numbers. Sadiki: “The land audit indicated that 72% was owned by white, and about 4% black owned. Now our minister has ordered that we do a phase three that will unbundle it further.” But Organized Agriculture, the land bank and many other organizations question the government's numbers. President of the World Farmers Organisation Dr. Theo de Jager explains why. De Jager: “The vast majority of farmers in South Africa do not trust that audit. It is not as easy as going to the deeds office and looking at the names there.” Chris: “Do we need to go further than the high panel investigation of former-president Kgalema Motlanthe? The problems with land reform are corruption, bureaucratic bungling - that report is there.” CLAIRE LINK: SINCE 1994, ONLY 21% OF FARMLAND IN FREEHOLD SOUTH AFRICA HAS BEEN TRANSFERRED FROM WHITE OWNERSHIP, BUT SOME ARGUE THAT SINCE LAND CLAIMANTS PREFERRED CASH OVER LAND, THAT PERCENTAGE COULD BE MUCH HIGHER. According to government 90% of land claims are currently settled through financial compensation. Dr. Vuyo: “The current status quo is not feasible, and if you start from that premise, and understanding THAT - there is no freedom without justice on land.” Farmers want the “just and equitable” compensation clause of the expropriation bill in the constitution to be more clearly defined as they would like market value for their properties. de Jager: “We are not scared about the expropriation, it’s about the compensation part of it. Because then we would know that there’s fair value being paid, nobody would be paid too much. Or too less in the process, and also it enables the land own owner who loses the land to re-establish himself elsewhere.” Steenkamp: “It’s the same as going to somebody and saying I’m taking away your future. 11:32:28 But not only taking away your future, but taking away all my farmer workers futures 11:32:34 and their children, you’re taking away families future, not only me. And as a whole in south Africa we’ve all seen where the rand as gone in the past few weeks, destructive and this thing will spiral dive until it’s resolved. 11:32:49 Sadiki: “We have spent 40 billion so far on restitution alone, which is very expensive, and I think at some point we need to agree that this exercise is going to take forever, and the constitution says government you have a responsibility to makes sure all your there’s access to land by all your citizens.” Mahlangu: “Government has tried to come up with many laws to be able to transform the land reform, but most of them have not been properly implemented, but also there’s been constitutional stumbling blocks.” Carte Blanche found that everyone was exceptionally guarded about the issue of expropriation without compensation, which only shows how difficult it is to separate emotions from this complex issue. Claire: “How would you like to see the expropriation of land without compensation roll out?” de Jager: “We should not expropriate any land without compensation. There’s just in no kind of democracy you can imagine, demanding from an individual to pick up the bill for a national imperative.” Mahlangu: “Land must be expropriated, but when it’s expropriate it let there be a thought process on how we’re going to do it” Chris: “Sometimes we wonder if the land question isn’t purposefully being held back so that the politicians have got a stick to beat ppl with.” Dr. Mahlati: “Land is emotional, we’re talking about social justice, identity and belonging. And if you don’t have land you don’t belong.”

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Johan Steenkamp’s farm is being expropriated. He’s a well-known avocado farmer and founder of Peppadew in South Africa. He is a co-owner of Akkerland Boerdery, which farms on two properties, Lukin and Salaita, near Njeledam behind Soutpansberg. His business partner is his brother-in-law, Arnold Cloete. He says they are happy to sell the land for fair market value, but they are currently involved in two court battles – one against the expropriation of land involving the Musekwa community, and another to fight the expropriation without compensation of our land. Akkerland Boerdery was originally offered an allegedly ridiculous amount of money as compensation, after the land was initially expropriated in favour of the Musekwa community. According to Steenkamp, the offer was neither reasonable nor accurate in terms of the market value of the property, and they started a process to ascertain the legality of the offer in court. Even before this expropriation process began, the new minister of rural development and land reform, Maite Nkoana-Mashabane, let Akkerland know their farms would be expropriated. The court documents were delivered a day before Easter weekend, and they were given just seven days to hand over the keys to their farms. After an emergency interdict against the minister, a process is now under way to set aside the entire expropriation process involving the two farms. The Musekwa community do not have a title deed to the Lukin and Salaita farms. The Kuvule community, by contrast, produced allegedly legitimate title deeds to the land long before the expropriation took place. Their lawyers, Denga Incorporated, have confirmed the view that it is in fact their clients who have actual rights to the land. But there are also allegations that the mining corporation Coal of Africa may in fact be behind the expropriation action, and that this has nothing to do with historical land reform, and everything to do with mining. It is common knowledge that the Lukin and Salaita farms form part of the valuable coal belt in the region. This is the where the land expropriate fight is currently taking place – it’s not theoretical. Please also see below that Steenkamps neighbour’s property was part of a land claim and it’s now in ruins – that community will also speak.
metadata.Summary: According to Ernst Roets of AfriForum, minister of land development and reform Maite Nkoana-Mashabane said they put together a list of 139 farms earmarked for land expropriation without compensation. This has become a hotly contested debate. In Limpopo nine farms are earmarked for expropriation - Akkerland Broerdery’s farm is on the Afriforum list, but AgriSA are questioning the legitimacy of the list, adding that making the list public was irresponsible. According to AgriSA, a snap survey of the list exposed its inaccuracy, which could have been legitimized before it was made public. Investigations conducted by AfriSA’s affiliations show that some farms on the list are those belonging to black farmers with joint procurement. We would also speak to AFASA in Midrand - who are the African Farmers Association of South Africa – who will say how this will also affect black farmers as well – not just white farmers, and there are black farmers on the list.
metadata.Further information: A detailed study shows how much land government owns, which could be used in land restitution – which is what Cyril Ramaphosa said earlier this year in SONA 2018. A preliminary constitutional review committee report shows 59% of submissions are not in favour of land expropriation, and Ralph Mathekga can talk about it (we already have the footage) - analysis on ANC and Parly headed for confrontation about above report. The ANC's own constituents don't list land ownership as their top 5 concerns. Zuma’s SONA 2017 address says 90% of people would prefer cash to land. The major concern is that government have failed in so many of its undertakings – especially its past land claim cases (for example the tea plantation next to Akkerland Broedery won the plantation in a land claim and it’s lying in ruin, that community will speak because no one assisted them in running it etc) Besides the obvious food security issues… The need for land restitution and a look at the success of the process – we would speak to experts: farmers weekly – who have a fair view on this issue – Chris Burgess – very progressive. And also Ralph Mathekga as well, and we would have the study. Land facts from the land audit report: comm. 5302 LINK: 17,439 million ha has been transferred from white ownership since 1994 – 21% of the 82,758 million ha of farmland in freehold SA. 27 feb 2018 National Assembly made landmark decision to review section 25 of the constitution in order to cater for the principle of land expropriation without compensation. This followed the decision by the ANC in December 2017 and the elective conference where it indicated it would start the process towards a constitutional amendment to make land redistribution possible without compensation – provided that it was sustainable and doesn’t harm the agricultural section or economy. What does the DATA say? Distributed: 4 850 100 ha Restored via restitution claims: 3 389 727 ha The equivalent area for which financial compensation was chosen is 2 772 457 ha Thus a total of 11 million ha have been redistributed through gov programs. The state owns more than 4,000 farms which makes up of 4,027 million ha according to 2015 State Land Audit. The total land moved out of white ownership = 15,039 million ha. LINK: This is because 90% of claimants opted for money rather than land – according to President Zuma in Sona 2017. Provincial land audits show, (research uni of Pretoria), that the department of rural development and land reform – ask Ralph Mathekga to explain… Roughly 17,439 MILLION HA has been transferred from white ownership since 1994. LINK: Only 4% of farms in south Africa generate a turnover of R5 million – most farms are in debt mostly 30-50% of their lands value. Who will inherit the debt? LINK: 80,000 land restitution claims have been lodged – 70% urban, 30% rural. It’s actually an urban issue. 94% of our country is registered at the deeds office – only 6% of our land is available… Land audit reveals whites own 72% of total farms and agricultural holdings – and africans own 4%. According to Chris: Not sure I understand about the interview. What info would you like me to send? I think the basic point is that the state has done close to bugger all about land reform for the last 23 years, and now wants to pin the problem on farmers. (We spent more money on protecting politicians last year, than buying farms for black farmers. That should about sum it up). The high-level report of former president Kgalema Monthlante also makes it crystal clear that the problem with land reform is corruption and mismanagement of the state, but that somehow never gets mentioned. We hosted the land summit out of sheer frustration and to showcase what commercial agriculture has achieved as far as transformational efforts are concerned, despite the state. The unintended result of the conference was an outpouring of goodwill from both black and white farmers, and a genuine willingness to make things work. The sort of constructive attitude that the state seems to purposefully and rather cynically sabotage for short term political gain. Bottom line is, if you want land reform to work, let the farmers do it (as Nick Serfontein, the big Free State farmer explained to Cyril in his open letter that went viral, and who today sits on the president’s advisory panel), because farmers know what it takes to farm. Bureaucrats in Pretoria don’t. Black farmers also need title to their land to be able to raise capital to fund their operations, which doesn’t happen. This is all not rocket science, but I think we truly underestimate how thoroughly useless the state is, and the terrible danger that doing nothing holds for the entire country.
